newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Factory lockout reignites Cambodian labour unrest.
newsitem.headline: Factory lockout reignites Cambodian labour unrest.

text.p: More than 3,000 workers were locked out of Cambodia's largest garment factory on Thursday when they demanded better working conditions, sparking the third labour protest in a week in the capital.
Human rights workers said it was the largest demonstration in Cambodia since December 1991, when student protests were put down with violence in Phnom Penh.

Workers for Cambodia Garments Ltd, led by opposition politician Sam Rainsy and chiefs of their new union, marched peacefully about 10 km (six miles) from their factory to the Council of Ministers, the National Assembly and the palace, where King Norodom Sihanouk agreed to meet the workers on Friday morning.

The labour unrest, which followed demonstrations on Sunday and Tuesday, has prompted the Ministry of Industry to hold meetings with factory management and caused the cancellation of a visit to the factory by a Hong Kong trade delegation.
But Kong Yee Cheng, executive director of Cambodia Garments, denied worker allegations of long hours, low pay and poor conditions.
He told Reuters the lockout occurred because "some workers want to work, but others don't," adding that he was concerned about acts of sabotage.

At the National Assembly, parliamentarians from the three major parties met with the three women who head the Free Trade Union of Khmer Workers and two male union representatives to discuss their demands.

Union chiefs told parliamentarians they wanted the right to organise freely, salary increases from $35 to $50 per month, a 40-hour work week, three months' paid maternity leave, job security, insurance coverage and a stop to what they said was physical and verbal abuse at Cambodia Garments.

The demonstration broke up after more than six hours, when Sam Rainsy, who backed the formation of the union on December 10, announced the 3,000 workers would reconvene later on Thursday at their factory to meet with management.

A protest at the factory on Tuesday, which started after the three union chiefs said they were suspended from work, prompted guards to shoot into the air to stop journalists and workers from entering the factory compound.
There are 34 garment factories in Cambodia employing more than 16,000 workers, according to the Industry Ministry.
While the government has embraced new companies, rights groups have said the workers are not treated fairly.
Last week Thomas Hammarberg, special representative of the U.N. Secretary-General for Human Rights in Cambodia, called working conditions in garment factories appalling.
